subsubtopic: WINNIPEG PEACE WALK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Liberal Task Force on Peace, Security and World Disarmament began its first week of public hearings to consult with Canadians from coast to coast on Canada's future role with respect to peace, security, and world disarmament.
The Winnipeg Co-ordination Committee for Disarmament presented a very thorough and comprehensive brief to our committee. That committee represents a coalition of over 30 organizations working for peace. The committee made many good recommendations, some of which need to be urgently and seriously considered.
The Winnipeg Co-ordination Committee for Disarmament is holding its fourth annual Walk for Peace in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on Saturday, June 8, 1985 at 11.30 a.m., beginning in front of the Legislature. Its representatives have asked me to extend an invitation to Members of Parliament and Senators from the three political parties, and any other Canadians who wish to express their concern for peace, to join them on Saturday, June 8, in Winnipeg.

Mr. Speaker, in recognition of Environment Week, June 2 to 8, I wish to raise a matter which concerns all Canadians.

June 3, 1985
In this age of industrialization we must constantly seek ways to ensure that the rules and regulations which are laid out for the safety of our citizens are followed. We also have a responsibility to protect those citizens who carry out their civic duty and report the illegal or unethical activities of which they have knowledge.
For example, if an employee knows that his or her employer is dumping toxic wastes illegally, the first step is to approach the management directly. If the employer then tells him or her to keep quiet or risk losing his or her job, the person is faced with a moral dilemma. The choice is to say nothing and keep the job, or to blow the whistle and risk losing the job.
The people who blow the whistle should be protected from dismissal or other retaliatory measures. These are people who are convinced that there are illegal or unethical activities going on, and have been specifically directed to say nothing.
A "Whistle Blowers' Protection Act" would ensure that the people who step forward to report such activities are not punished. They should not have to pay, in real terms, by losing their jobs, their seniority, or financial security, as a result of making the public aware, as it is the public's right to know of potentially hazardous situations.
It is time for us to examine the necessity of bringing in legislation to protect such civic minded people.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to tell the House about a letter which was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), with a copy to me, concerning the Budget. The letter comes from Cathy Syse, a constituent of mine, who is a secretary in Winnipeg. She has been working for nine years, grosses $15,204 a year, and nets $12,376. She wants the Prime Minister to understand better how middle working class people live. She wrote in part:
The following list are the payments that I have to make this year. Rent $4,140; hydro $360; telephone $240; gasoline $1,440; food $2,040; cigarettes $780; liquor $120; insurance $500.
The balance of $2,756 has to go for clothes, entertainment, Christmas and increases in my rent, food etc.
The car that I am driving is a 1973 model and I haven't bought any new furniture for the last five years. My holidays are spent sitting at home and I don't go to nightclubs or out for dinner because it's too expensive.
1 simply cannot afford this new Budget of Mr. Wilson's. Perhaps Mr. Wilson can draw up a budget for me so that I can afford this new federal Budget.
I am a simple average working person with very few luxuries-and now you want to tax the only luxuries I have so that I won't be able to afford them either. Is that what you had in mind?
I doubt Mr. Prime Minister if you will ever read this letter or if I'll even get some sort of reply. It will probably be thrown in the garbage-

I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his
time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take advantage of this opportunity to draw the attention of the House to the fact that this week, from June 2 to June 8, is Canadian Environment Week. One priority has been set aside for each day: parks, wildlife, research, volunteers, acid rain and hazardous products.

The purpose is to demonstrate how each affects the environment.
The reason I think this is important is because I represent the South West Nova area which is known for its beautiful beaches, rivers, lakes, and unspoiled lands. I realize that I am not the only Canadian who is blessed with such magnificent natural gifts in his backyard.
We have to be vigilant if we want to protect our environment. The threat of acid rain is real, and only through co-operation can we achieve success.
The point I want to make is that the concern for an improved environment is everybody's responsibility. [Translation]
We can all, by our behaviour, help improve the environment: from the driver who can demand unleaded gas to industries that have a responsibility to control the environmental consequences of their activities.

Each and every one of us has a responsibility and I am very pleased that the theme for the Canadian Environment Week is "Environment... A Shared Responsibility".

[ Translation]

subtopic: DEMANDS OF CONFEDERATION OF FAMILY GROUPS OF QUEBEC

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: DEMANDS OF CONFEDERATION OF FAMILY GROUPS OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after making a number of attempts to arrange a meeting with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Quebec Confederation of Family Agencies has yet to receive a favourable reply.
That is at least what was reported in La Presse on May 8. The organization in question, referred to as COFAQ, is an umbrella organization for fourteen federations of family agencies across Quebec, and had asked for an urgent meeting with the Minister of Finance to inform him of the concerns of Quebecers with respect to the Minister's "sacrifice Budget".
The Confederation is asking for a Budget that is fair and
equitable for our families. It is also asking that child tax
credits and family allowances be left intact.
June 3, 1985

Everyone knows that family agencies have a reputation for being understanding and cooperative. However, Mrs. Denise Laporte-Dubuc has informed the Minister of Finance that if he did not take their recommendations into consideration, the COFAQ would feel obliged to react by organizing a demonstration in Ottawa after Budget Day.
I hope the Minister, who claims his Government is one that consults, considered the requests made by the Confederation of Quebec Family Agencies.

subtopic: COMMITMENT TO IMPROVE MANAGEMENT OF TAX REVENUE
COMMITMENT TO IMPROVE MANAGEMENT OF TAX REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a taxpayer I was delighted to hear in the Budget of the Government's commitment to manage more effectively, as evidenced by its undertaking to improve cash management and to dispose of unneeded property.
I am sure the Government will also move quickly to correct the numerous other areas of mismanagement and misspending which were identified by the Auditor General in his 1984 report, including the misclassification of public servants which he estimated costs us all $125 million each year.
In addition, 1 was pleased to learn of the progress which is being made by the Task Force on Program Review which is headed by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen). That task force is aimed at simplifying programs and eliminating duplication. It is a task force which should produce not just millions, but billions of dollars in savings that should be reflected in a lower deficit next year.
Improving government management is the key to ensuring that our tax dollars are being spent as effectively and as efficiently as possible. I am never really happy, as a taxpayer, to pay taxes, but the next time I write a cheque to the Receiver General of Canada I will feel a lot better to know that my tax dollars are not being wasted.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) delusions of grandeur keep growing. I am referring to a newspaper article on Friday which stated that, from now on, when the Prime Minister travels abroad it will be with two aircraft, one for him and one for the press. I guess two jets constitute an "airfarce".
The way the new system will work is that the plane with the press in it will touch down first. Then, all the journalists will run to position themselves, and wait for the great event. Finally, the announcement will come-"The ego has landed".
The Prime Minister brags about being able to pick up the telephone and talk to Ronald Reagan any time, but I think it's
Uncle Ronnie who does the talking. He tells the Prime Minister how to act like a President. "Get your own podium", Ronald Reagan says, and presto, the Prime Minister has a podium. "Get your wife her own office and staff', and presto, the Prime Minister's wife is installed in the Langevin Block. "Pretend that you are the head of state when I come to call; it will make for better television", and presto, the Governor General is not even invited to Quebec City. What is next, a helicopter pad at 24 Sussex?
The latest advice from Uncle Ronnie is that separate planes will help in news management. For once maybe the President is right. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) does need two aircraft when he travels: one for himself, and one for his ego.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-DENIAL OF EMIGRATION TO SOVIET JEWS
U.S.S.R.-DENIAL OF EMIGRATION TO SOVIET JEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few nights ago I attended a very moving ceremony in Willowdale, presented by the National Council of Jewish Women. The guest speaker was our Ambassador to the U.N., Mr. Stephen Lewis. In an eloquent, dignified ceremony, 14 Canadian students in cap and gown received graduation diplomas on behalf of 14 Soviet Refusenik students who were denied the right to Jewish religious education and university admittance. These are basic rights we take for granted in Canada and the western world.
In his address Ambassador Lewis stressed five key points to help Soviet Jewry. Each Member should continue to speak up in Parliament for human rights; the issue should be stressed through quiet diplomatic manoeuvres; the issue of human rights should be kept at the forefront of bilateral negotiations; debates in international forums, as my colleague for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) did so effectively at the U.N., and through human rights conferences such as those currently taking place in Ottawa; public pressure should be kept up by keeping their cause alive every day.
The gravity of this issue is illustrated by an important fact. In 1979 some 51,000 Soviet Jews were allowed to leave, while in 1984 the number was only 876. I applaud the tremendous and courageous action taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in Russia this spring. As a Government we must continue to press the Soviet Government to release another 50,000 Jews. This would show the world the good will of the U.S.S.R. and its humanitarian interest in family reunification.

June 3, 1985

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) has been caught with a snout in the trough in the latest incident of pork-barrelling.
The people of Newfoundland thought they had left the merchant family mentality behind after 1949, but now it appears the Minister of Justice is trying to revive the good old tradition. A merchant family, as we know, must have one member in business, one in government, and a few scattered around the courts. The Minister's family has one member who is a prominent businessman, and from whom Revenue Canada is now claiming $380,000. Both of the Minister's sons are legal agents for the Department of Justice, courtesy of their father, and have as their responsibilities the task of acting on behalf of Revenue Canada.
The question is: will the Minister's sons, who were named as federal legal agents by their father, act to prosecute the uncle, who is their father's brother, and who owes the Government of Canada $380,000?
This whole incident gives new meaning to the theory of relativity, and this outrageous conflict of interest makes Billy-gate look mild by comparison. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) ought to relieve the Minister of Justice of his responsibilities until this whole mess can be cleared up and corrected.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal and NDP Members of the House are demoralized and confused. For years Liberal Budgets put Canada deeper and deeper into debt, reaching a total of $200 billion, with an annual deficit of $38 billion. They threw money around like drunken drug addicts. For example, they sent a secretary to the Riviera to improve her French, and threw millions of dollars at jobs which actually increased the number of unemployed, and so when the PC Budget, (1), reduced the deficit and started Canada on a free enterprise road, by creating a climate and providing incentives for small business that will encourage investment, and which will mean jobs instead of increasing the debt; and (2), it offered a glad hand of co-operation to all provinces, instead of the former one finger salute with policies which crippled their industries; and (3), it placed a surtax on corporations and the banks, along with a notice to the wealthy that a minimum tax is coming later instead of destroying incentive by heavy taxation, the Liberal and NDP went into a mad frenzy. They moan because interest rates are down, and weep because the deficit is decreasing. Yes, their negativism and confusion are evident every day. But who cares? The people of Canada are happy because the Budget is the beginning of a new and prosperous Canada, a Canada
which will pay its debts. So I say, down with the negative opposition, and up with the people!
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS AFFECTING OLD AGE PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister I will put my question to the Minister of Finance. Like thousands of other Canadians, I suppose, I received a letter from the Hon. Member for Pembina suggesting that Canadians write to myself and the Hon. Member for Oshawa urging us to take the heat off the Prime Minister as a result of the Budget. The Hon. Member says in the letter: "I would not even think about writing you now except that the situation in Ottawa is critical. If we don't help, our Prime Minister will have great difficulty." 1 will have to have some private consultations with the Hon. Member for Oshawa to see how we respond.
June 3, 1985

The Minister of Finance knows that, as a result of his Budget and the deindexation of old age pensions, the value of an old age pension by the year 1990 will be lower by $30 a month in real terms. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 speak in sorrow and in anger with the Government for its absolute and abysmal failure to live up to the explicit promises it made during the election campaign to the charities, to the voluntary sector of the country, to take action on the proposals which was and is called "give and take". It is just one more of the many promises, sacred and otherwise, that the Tory Government has broken.
June 3, 1985

The give-and-take proposal, as it is called, provides for a 50 per cent tax rebate on what people contribute to charity regardless of their income. For example, for every one dollar a Canadian gives to charity, that contributor would receive a rebate of 50 cents on their income tax return. This would have the benefit of equalizing the cost of giving by offering equal incentives to all regardless of earnings and the rate at which they are taxed.
At present, as 1 think we all know, the higher one's income, the more benefit one receives from being able to deduct charitable donations at a higher tax rate. For example, right now a person who earns $50,000 per year and gives $200 to charity will be able to get back $100 because he is taxed at 50 per cent. A person who now earns $30,000 per year who gives the same $200, which is taxed at 30 per cent, will only be able to deduct 30 per cent of his or her gift, so that that person will only get back $60 rather than $100. It is unequal and unfair that one person gets back $100 and the other gets back $60. It is unfair that the one who earns more gets back more. The give-and-take proposal would equalize the benefits to all Canadians and of course encourage them to give more to charity.
Because the give-and-take proposal would encourage more people to give to charity, it would also secure larger memberships in charitable organizations and more participation in the voluntary sector. There is a proven relationship between one's giving and one's participation. It is a well-known axiom that where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
During the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a promise which was printed in the bulletin of the umbrella organization that relates to the voluntary sector. The bulletin reads:
We are committed to implementing a Tax Credit equal to a percentage of donations made to registered charities.
That was a firm commitment and it is here in black and white. Tory Members made this promise or, as they called it, commitment, but that was when the Prime Minister was in opposition and running for office. That was before the election. Since that time, he has become the Prime Minister. Where is this promise after almost nine months? Of course, the place for this promise to have been kept was in the Budget.
Voluntary organizations across the country waited for an announcement. Where is this announcement? Where is the give-and-take tax credit program in the Budget recently tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)? It has vanished. It is not to be seen and not to be heard.
The Opposition of old has now become the Government and, abracadabra, it has become a Government of magic vanishing acts. With the Prime Minister, now you see it, now you don't. Not only did we not get jobs, jobs, jobs, but we did get promises, promises, promises which have been broken, broken, broken. The Prime Minister has done it again, and three million volunteers working for 40,000 charities now know the value of the promises made by the Prime Minister.
The Budget-Mr. de Corneille
What about the Secretary of State (Mr. McFean)? He made the give-and-take proposal his pet crusade while he was on the opposition side. Let us take a look at a few of the promises he made. It would require days and even weeks to recite them all to you, Mr. Speaker. I can hardly do justice to all of the commitments and promises made by my hon. friend on the issue of give and take. For example, when he was in opposition, the present Secretary of State said the following:
We are committed to a fundamental realignment of the tax treatment for charitable giving-the principle of a charitable tax credit-which will offer equitable incentives to all taxpayers to support their charities.
In other words, he said that he was entirely for the give-and-take proposal. He also said that the voluntary sector was the largest employer of lower and middle-class Canadians, and he was right when he said that. In addressing the voluntary sector, he said the following:
You (the Voluntary Sector) offer many less advantaged Canadians a bridge to employment. Canada's Voluntary Sector is an untapped resource that not only can reduce government spending but can actually create jobs in the process.
This is why we are committed to a principle of a charitable tax credit, to a tax environment which will offer equitable incentives. Give and take is on the agenda.
He said that give and take was on the agenda. Where is it on the Tory agenda? Is it only on the Tory agenda when Tory Members are in opposition? Now we have a Tory Government but we do not see that promise. Give and take was on the agenda of the Secretary of State when he was the Conservative critic for this area and spoke to the National Voluntary Organizations in the spring of 1984. All of the quotations which I have just read come from that one particular speech addressed to the National Voluntary Organizations.
Give and take was on the agenda then. Only a year ago, the Secretary of State told us that it was on his talking agenda, his speaking agenda, his promises agenda and his "get-the-Tories-elected" agenda. Where has the give-and-take proposal gone? Is the Secretary of State a magician as well? It appears as though we had another vanishing act here. I could paper my office with the promises made by the Secretary of State throughout his years in the House of Commons. He made promises not only in the House of Commons but in committees and in speeches to voluntary organizations across the country. Whenever he had a chance, he made these promises.
It is interesting to note that in 1980, the Secretary of State told us that the Government must act on this issue on behalf of the voluntary organizations "to provide voluntary agencies with financial aid to support their fund-raising activities". Then in 1982 he told us not to think "of the decrease this would bring to federal coffers but to think of this as an engine for employment creation". Those were the words of the Secretary of State. As far back as five years ago, the Secretary of State was telling us that the voluntary sector needed this give-and-take program so that it could create jobs.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) insists that, above all, his Budget is designed to create jobs. If so, why did the Secretary of State not tell the Minister of Finance about this marvellous way to create jobs? It is a marvellous way to create jobs. If the sorrow of the Secretary of State was so great, why

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. de Corneille
did he not cry on the shoulder of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty), on the shoulder of the Minister of Finance or on the shoulder of the Prime Minister in order to make sure that give and take really got on the agenda as he promised? I am afraid his tears were crocodile tears. Now that Tory Members have been elected on the basis of their election promises, they can forget all of them.
The Secretary of State accused the past Government of being guilty of a stark contrast between words and deeds, rhetoric and action, but the former Liberal Government never made a promise to instate the give-and-take proposal. However, the Secretary of State and the Prime Minister did make that promise. They are the ones who are guilty of rhetoric rather than action.
Is this House an echo chamber? Indeed, the Secretary of State really shot himself in his foot with his own words, words which I am sure he wishes the voluntary agencies and charities across the country would quickly forget.
The Secretary of State saved the best for last. On December 7, 1983, the Throne Speech of the Liberal Government proposed to set up a joint parliamentary task force consisting of Members of the House of Commons and the other place to consider all issues related to formulating an appropriate definition of a charity and what a charity could do under the Income Tax Act, in order to speed up the possibility of moving toward the consideration of the give-and-take program. The Liberal Government realized that it was an important issue to resolve. It was important enough to be in the Throne Speech. What happened to the proposal? Did it have an opportunity in its important work? Clearly the answer is no. It was obstructed by the present Secretary of State. He blocked the formation of the task force. He said that it was not good enough for the Liberal Government to deal only with the important definition of a charity. The Secretary of State maintained that he wanted a package deal. He wanted to tie it to the consideration of give and take. His position was: unless there was a discussion of give and take, then there would be no consideration given to the definition of charities. According to the Secretary of State, the agenda of the task force had to be all or nothing at all.
At the National Voluntary Organizations consultation meeting in 1984, the Secretary of State was heard loud and clear on the issue. Quoting from a copy of his speech which he circulated to. members of the National Voluntary Organizations:
Just last Thursday, the Hon. Serge Joyal called to discuss the task force and to seek Progressive Conservative Party support for a resolution in both the House of Commons and the Senate.
The present Secretary of State continued:
I have responded that quick agreements can be achieved, if the frame of reference is broadened to address the fiscal framework as well as the legal. Your tax proposal should be part of the reference, not just the definition of charities.
The Liberal Government was blocked by the present Secretary of State and the Tories from doing anything constructive in attempting to resolve the issue of an appropriate definition
of charities for income tax purposes. It was a very important issue, and it still is.
The Secretary of State cannot be proud that he, the most vocal spokesman for the Tories for voluntary organizations, should have blocked the progress of the former Government. He made promise after promise and then blocked action on the very things which he had promised were most dear to his heart. That was unconscionable.
In 1985 the Tories formed the Government. Finally, the first Budget was brought down. What is in it? 1 can hardly believe it. The Tories have decided to do something about part of the issue of the definition of charities for income tax purposes. Wonder of wonders. The Secretary of State blocked the former Government from forming an all-Party committee to consider the whole definition of charities, including the political activities which they would be allowed and many other complex aspects of what constitutes a charity. It is now a year later. What have we got? We have less than that which he blocked the former Government from doing. It does not include the former Government's proposal of a fiscal give-and-take program. Where is the give and take? It is not even on the agenda. It has vanished by Tory magic. One and a half years later, voluntary organizations are less well off than they might have been. They owe that to the man who was purported to have fought the hardest for them, the present Secretary of State. It is unbelievable. It is a "now you see it, now you don't", brought to us by the Tories. "Give and take" the proposal is called. That is precisely what the Tories have done. They promised to give but have taken away what they promised. The Secretary of State has found a new way of communicating on the issue-absolute silence. Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard him speak one word in the House on give and take since the Tories were elected? You haven't, not a word. Why did he not dig in his heels the way he did with the previous Government and say to the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Finance, or the Prime Minister that he wants a fiscal and legal framework, a definition of charities, and give and take considered in one package? Now that he is in government where are the eloquent speeches and demands? Silence, like the silence of the Berlin Wall.
Did the Tories think they could get away with this? Apparently they did. They thought they could distract attention from broken promises by offering partial action on the definition of charities to voluntary organizations. They thought the National Voluntary Organizations, its constituent organizations, and some 40,000 voluntary organizations in Canada, would buy the pay-off to forget.
The press release from the National Voluntary Organizations and reactions from a number of societies, associations and churches show that they are not amused. The Government will be hearing from them. The Tories' sop to voluntary organizations and charities has not worked. The Tories have underestimated the wisdom of such organizations if they believe that they can get away with this ruse. It will not work. The people of Canada are too smart for the Tory shell game. Regarding the give-and-take tax credit program for charitable
June 3, 1985

organizations in Canada, the Tories gave and the Tories have taken away. Blasted be the game of the Tories!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise today, on the sixth day of the budget debate, to support the measures announced in the Budget by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
For almost 14 years I have experienced the ups and downs of trying to run a small business in my riding of London East.
I think it is extremely important that this Budget reflects the views, not of politicians, but of Canadians from all regions and many backgrounds who have brought their different perspectives to Ottawa to serve the national interest.
As a small businessman, I believe that the collective wisdom of the market-place must be given priority that it has not received in the past. To restore a body to health and to make it grow, the first requirement is nourishment. At long last our economy is now receiving more than the temporary band-aid solutions of the past. Although these might have provided some short-term relief, they only dealt with the surface problems and not the root causes.
Small businessmen, and indeed most Canadians who have experienced the problems first hand, realize the previous approach has not worked and the time has come for a new direction. We believe this Budget reflects the views of the Canadian people because we have benefited from the collective wisdom of many Canadians from across Canada who have generously shared their views with us these past months.
In rising to speak in the budget debate, 1 can tell the people of London East that the commitment for change that was made to them by our Party has taken a progressive step forward. The discussion surrounding the Budget projects two emergent themes. The first of these reflects the approach of the previous administration. That approach was rejected by the Canadian people. It consists of judging Government by what it gives out. Members of the Opposition Parties are telling each Canadian to look at the Budget and ask what it does for them personally rather than looking at it collectively in the best interests of all Canadians.
This approach did not accomplish what it hoped to achieve in the previous Government, although 1 am sure it was brought in with the best of intentions. It did nothing to encourage investment and create jobs and opportunity, but rather saddled our recovery with a debt load that now absorbs one of every three dollars paid by Canadian taxpayers.
I ask both my Liberal and NDP colleagues in the House to consider looking at the Budget from a more positive and objective viewpoint. The questions that should be asked in order to arrive at an objective evaluation of the merits of the Budget look at it as a whole and with the big picture in mind. We all realize that the prime function of the Budget is to begin the process of restoring confidence in our business communities and our country. A working economy reduces employment and will allow the Government to provide effective protection and renewed hope for those experiencing the perils of a struggling economy,
In view of the critical state of our economy, 1 believe the
time has come to put aside the temptation to score political

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Jepson
points and to work together in the best interests of all Canadians. The best thing about our Budget is its realistic approach to alleviating Canada's problems of unemployment and economic inertia. This has to be the focus of any responsible Budget because these fundamental problems lead directly to the countless serious problems experienced by Canadians that the Government is committed to assisting.
This Budget is a realistic answer to the record of the last Government. That Government was faced with serious problems and decided that a strategy of massive government spending would be the best route to go. However, we still have the problems of unemployment, a spiralling debt, and a structural deficit which has limited the opportunity for recovery.
I would like to speak to this Budget from the perspective of a small businessman. Everyone knows the importance of this sector. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business estimates that it creates at least 80 per cent of all new lasting jobs. The key to a healthy economy is a healthy small business sector. The health of the small business sector depends on the commercial environment which is, to a great extent, determined by the tax framework. This has a direct influence on the willingness of people to invest, of businessmen to take risks, on the flexibility and supply of labour, and on the ability of consumers to buy.
Today I will focus my remarks on the effectiveness of the Budget in changing the tax structure into one that will allow small businesses to start the process of economic renewal. The single most impressive change announced in the Budget is the long overdue measure that extends to all Canadians a $500,000 lifetime exemption from capital gains. In 1972, on the recommendation of the 1966 Royal Commission on Taxation, the taxation of capital gains was introduced primarily in the interest of equity. The decision at that time to include only one-half of capital gains as taxable income reflected the concern that such a tax would have some adverse effects on the economy. Furthermore, the erosion of the cost base of assets by inflation was also regarded as something that should be compensated for.
In 1985 it is appropriate to adjust this legislation because of the circumstances. The balance has shifted in a way that makes it necessary to use new measures to encourage investment and enterprise, thereby creating jobs and opportunities for Canadians. Businessmen and women are not taking the initiatives that will lead to the growth of our economy, but with this Budget, we believe they will.
The capital gains tax made it less attractive to make equity investments. The system allows a limited deductibility of capital losses which are particularly significant during a recessionary period. The hidden tax effect of inflation has already been mentioned as creating a taxable capital gain on paper even when an asset has actually lost value. Finally, the capital gains system tends to lock in investments, or to inhibit their investment altogether.
The point of these observations is that the capital gains exemption gives small business a more just return on the risks they have taken with the hope that they, in turn, will invest
and expand in their business, thereby creating more jobs and opportunities for Canadians. If money invested in a small business is given a better rate of return, we believe that more money will be invested than has been in the past.
A final point I would like to make with respect to capital gains concerns the signal it sends to all Canadians. All of the measures in the Budget, but particularly this one, tell people that we are counting on them to go out and do well. If people get the feeling that they can succeed by using their resources, then this Budget has accomplished a great deal.
Reflecting their grave doubts about the character of the Canadian people, the Opposition say that the capital gains exemption will only result in rich people benefiting from the purchase of a Florida condominium. We are different as a Progressive Conservative Government. We have great faith in the Canadian people, that they will respond to those initiatives and share this opportunity with all Canadians.
Unfortunately, they do not seem to make the connection that the single most important reason for taking capital out of Canada and investing it in another country is a taxation and regulation environment that made Canada a bad place to invest. We say that Canada is a good place to invest and this will be reflected in the days ahead. Already, we have seen many positive economic signs in the market-place and sense a renewed feeling of confidence and optimism. FIR A tried to keep jobs in Canada, but in the long run it destroyed them by making other countries more attractive places to invest. This was the same short sighted philosophy underlying the National Energy Program and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax.
In 1985, Canada is turning into one of the best places to invest because of the confidence we have shown in the decision-making of consumers and business persons alike. Two years from now, we believe the Opposition will be surprised to see how Canadians of all income levels have responded in a positive way to invest in their own country. We believe in Canadians. A capital gains exemption will not mean much if there is no money available to be invested. The Budget addresses this question and contains a number of measures that compliment the exemption in ways that will channel the benefits toward the ordinary Canadian. The Budget opens a number of new sources for investment capital that will find its way into investments that will create jobs.
Venture capital funds patterned after the Quebec Federation of Labour Fund will be encouraged by the Budget. This is a direct instrument, to benefit both labour and small business, that will be advanced by the extension of a generous tax credit for people taking advantage of this opportunity. Investment tax credits have been recognized as one of the most positive ways to encourage entry into the market. This credit will bring the coverage up to a possible 40 per cent of the value of the investment. Sixty per cent of this investment will go into the equity of the small and medium-sized Canadian businesses.
The innovative Quebec Federation of Labour program that inspired this measure has been a genuine success story. Le
June 3, 1985

Fonds de Solidarite des Travailleurs du Quebec was the initiative of workers who wanted to help themselves out of the doldrums of the recession. The Quebec fund has been in operation for two years and has been a significant benefit to participants, both for its investment value and as a tax credit. Furthermore, it has been said to have provided Quebecers with
1,000	jobs through the impetus it provides for the economy.
This measure has been largely ignored by the Opposition speakers, which I suppose is the highest endorsement we would expect from them. Since it is a tax credit, this is a very progressive instrument to bring about the objective of labour participation in business equity. It will also present the opportunity for people with lower income to take advantage of their lifetime capital gains exemption. It is hard to say whether the investors or the businesses will benefit more from this, but it is good to see policies that do not lopsidedly distribute benefits while taxing the system as a whole. I hope all Members will join me in congratulating the Minister of Finance for extending this innovative proposal. I believe that it merits encouragement as something that will be of great economic significance to all regions of Canada.
Another progressive measure announced in the Budget was raised in the course of the exhaustive consultation process. Both the Canadian Organization of Small Business and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business strongly recommend the making available of certain pension funds to provide equity for small business. The availability of several billion dollars for equity financing will have considerable impact in making our small business sector one that will be able to respond to changing technologies and market conditions. By giving small business both the incentive and the opportunity to increase its equity, the Budget has taken a giant step forward to achieving a secure economic renewal.
A key to any competitive economy in the next few decades will be the priority it places on high technology and research. Both Japan and West Germany have recognized this and their economies reflect it. Unfortunately, our social and economic policies in the past have ail but ignored the need for a thoughtful approach to fostering innovation that can both be developed and applied to the manufacturing process. Other major industrialized economies average close to twice Canada's proportionate expenditure in R and D as a percentage of Gross National Product. The R and D tax credit for small businesses consists of 35 per cent of research and development spending up to a total of $700,000. This credit will be refundable in full to the company that uses it. This will make it a much more direct benefit, since only 40 per cent was refundable in the past.
The resources for this program are closely focused on the small business sector. This is a progressive step because this money will get some operations off the ground that would not otherwise have existed. If an economy is to adjust to a format that is both specialized and flexible, this is exactly the sort of policy that we need. The essence of the idea of competition is efficiency, that is the most productivity for a given level of available resources. I believe the specific tax measures
The Budget-Mr. Jepson
described in the Budget serve very valuable policy objectives. At the same time, it is good to see that the system itself will get a comprehensive review through the corporate income tax system discussion paper.
In the pre-Budget consultation, representatives of the business community never objected to paying their fair share of tax, but they did wonder why the system had to be so complicated. This was seen as a cost in the same way that high tax rates area. A complicated tax system absorbs time, energy and expense. It deeply affects the profile of corporate structures and planning for both small and large businesses. Our Government is sensitive to the problems created by a complicated tax system.
Let me conclude my remarks with some observations on the deficit. All thinking Canadians realize that we cannot continue to spend beyond our means, but we cannot accomplish this reduction overnight. We must, at the same time, maintain that high level of effective social programs which is important to all of us. The Minister of Finance considered this carefully, and I support the resulting Budget. Important programs have been maintained and the tax level remains at an equitable level. At the same time, we have launched a vigorous program to reduce the level of our deficit.
Budget '85 is an historic change for Canadian Government; it charts a bold new direction, rightfully placing responsibility in the hands of the private sector. This is the only basis for a strong and viable economy. I urge all Members to avoid spreading fear and to join the Government in supporting a Budget that is clearly setting a new, positive direction for Canada. It is a direction that will utilize the vast and rich natural and human resources we possess in this country and that have been left untapped for far too long.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a couple of comments on the speech by the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson). I think there are some basic inequities in the Budget that I do not believe Members of the Government have accepted or understand. He is defending the fact that the capital gains exemption will now allow people to make $500,000 in capital gains without paying any tax at all. What he does not speak about is from where that money is going to come. It will come from the imposition of deindexing the old age pension.
That will go on year after year. It is $100 a year for a pensioner in 1986; $200 in 1987; and $300 in 1988. You can double the amount for a couple both receiving the old age pension. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or his colleagues say that pensioners have to contribute to bring down the deficit, the fact is that is not true. Pensioners are being asked to make that contribution from the pittance on which they have to live to finance this enormous tax exemption on capital gains, a tax exemption which will rise to more than $1 billion a year within the course of two or three years. It starts small and gets bigger and bigger.

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Jepson
It is argued by the Government that that is OK because it is putting a surtax on people who are well off, on corporations and the banks in 1986. That is correct, but what the Government does not say is that it is for only one year. The benefits in terms of the tax exemption on capital gains will go on in perpetuity if this Government has a chance to stay in office. The cost to pensioners in order to take tax off the rich will go on in perpetuity.
Is it any wonder that millions of Canadians are skeptical about the Budget? They look at the fact that the Canadian association for small business, big business, corporate presidents, people in the investment community on Bay Street and St. James Street were amply consulted. The pensioners' organizations and organizations representative of the aged were either not consulted at all, or what they had to say was completely ignored, Mr. Speaker.
How can the Hon. Member defend in glowing terms a Budget which on the face of it is so inequitable? It takes from the poor, particularly the elderly poor, and particularly from that group of women who are 65 or over, widowers, separated or divorced and who have only one income. They will have to pay for the tax exemption on speculation in real estate, art and perhaps the occasional investment in small business. Is that really fair? I ask the Hon. Member to defend that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his question. We believe it is a fair Budget. We believe that with the election of 211 Government Members, people were telling us very clearly that it was time for a change in the economic policy of Canada and that it was time to make some of those hard decisions.
As I have studied this Budget, I believe the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated on distributing those changes in a very fair and equitable way. I believe all Canadians, including seniors, are prepared to make those sacrifices in the short term to look for the long-term benefits, benefits that will not be there when many people reach retirement because the pension funds have been seriously depleted, and virtually exhausted, covering the massive debt we have had to finance these last years.
1 would suggest to the Hon. Member there is an overwhelming feeling that we must come to grips with this debt and make sure that we have a vibrant and secure economy to allow those Canadians in the years ahead, when it comes time for them to retire, funds for their retirement and security.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson). Has the Hon. Member read the article in The Citizen dated May 30, 1985, under the heading, "Federal Budget presents problems for small business"? The article in part reads:
The small business community might have been too quick to sing the praises of last week's federal budget, a panel of Ottawa tax experts said Wednesday.
The article goes on:
The only jobs that are sure to be in demand as a direct result of the Budget are those of professional tax advisers-because many of the measures will be hard to understand without professional advice.
And because some of the measures go only halfway-for example, increasing the limits of registered retirement savings plan contributions without allowing entrepreneurs or their relatives to invest RRSP funds in their own businesses- they are virtually useless for small business.
Could the Hon. Member comment on such a statement?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his question, Mr. Speaker. I did not see the article in the paper. I did speak to Mr. John Bulloch, who heads up the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, who is representative, 1 would say, of a clear majority of small businesses in Canada. Mr. Bulloch was overwhelmingly impressed with the Budget. He sees it as a real vehicle, as a springboard for the economy for small businesses to create jobs. He is looking with great anticipation, as are I believe most Canadians, to the positive results that will come.
Let me underline to the Hon. Member that this is not an overnight situation. It will take time. We as a Government are clearly saying to the people that we have faith in them and faith in the business community. We have a country that is rich both in human and national resources and we trust the business sector to play a large role in the recovery. We have every confidence that it will do so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak at this very critical time. It seems to me that what this new so-called Progressive Conservative Government is doing with this Budget is beginning the destruction of the social security system which has been built up in Canada over the past 50 years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who are you trying to scare?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have seen one of those hidebound, old-fashioned-and when 1 am talking about old-fashioned, 1 am talking about a million years ago-Conservatives who just asked who I am trying to scare. I do not have to scare anybody. Any person, except a few of the very rich, who looks at this Budget will knows and recognizes that substantial cuts will result in every person's standard of living. Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker. I do not have to scare anybody.
We are back to debating some of the first principles which we thought we settled a long time ago on such matters as pension policies, social services and the support which Governments should give to those people in need. Let me bring to the attention of those Conservative Members who would like to ignore the real facts some of the very timely information which was contained in a report issued recently by the National Council of Welfare called Poverty on the Increase. Those are not my words. That is the title of a report put out by the National Council of Welfare.
Let me indicate briefly what this report says. This report indicates that Canadians have been hurt very badly by the recession. It reports that the decline in the number of people living in poverty which had been going on since 1969 has now
June 3, 1985

stopped. From 1981 to 1983, there has been a substantial increase in the number of people who are living in poverty. From 1981 to 1983, 600,000 more people were added to the number of Canadians living in poverty. We now have over four million Canadians living in poverty; a 24 per cent increase in two years.
One person in six in Canada is now living in poverty, a sharp increase from the best performance of a few years ago when one person in seven was living in poverty. This is a very significant deterioration. The Budget will compound the trend of the last couple of years and will prove to be a disaster for people in lower income brackets.
Let us look at what will happen to pensions. We have been repeatedly told that the deindexation of pensions will not reduce the living standards of pensioners in the next few years. I do not think, in the years I have served as a Member of Parliament, that we have ever made a more important decision than we did when we indexed old age pensions. I ask Lion. Members to think back to how the system operated before pensions were indexed. In particular, I remind Conservative Members that one of the biggest factors in defeating the Liberal Government, which was in office from 1945 to 1957, was that in 1956 or 1957 the then Liberal Government with its very great revenues was only prepared to increase pensions by $6 per month. The Conservative Leader who brought the Conservatives out of the wilderness and into Government for the first time in generations, Mr. Diefenbaker, went across the country, quite properly heaped scorn on the Liberals and called them; "Six-buck boys".
Mr. Diefenbaker won the election and increased pensions, but despite the calls by pensioners and people who spoke up for them, calling for fairly regular increases in pensions because the cost of living was rising, they did not get pension increases except in election years, at which time a Conservative or Liberal Government, trying to get support from pensioners, would increase pensions. One of the most important decisions made by any Canadian Parliament-and if 1 remember correctly, it was done with the unanimous support of all Parties then in Parliament-was to index pensions so that as the cost of living rose, the real standard of living of pensioners would not be reduced.
Now the Government has decided to deindex pensions. The only increase pensioners will receive will be if the increase in the cost of living rises by more than 3 per cent, at which point they will receive the difference between 3 per cent and the actual rate of inflation. This means that the standard of living for all people receiving OAS-and I am not talking about the Guaranteed Income Supplement-will be reduced by 3 per cent each year as long as we continue with this deindexation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unless inflation falls below 3 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 hear the Hon. Member's interjection. Inflation is now beginning to rise in the United States and in Canada. I ask Hon. Members to think of what this means to
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
someone who will retire this year at age 65. In five years-and more and more people are living longer-the real value of old age pensions will be reduced three times five, compounded, or by more than 15 per cent.
What about the person who is now 50 years of age and is thinking about how he or she will manage after reaching retirement age at 65? They had every reason to believe that they would receive their Canada Pension, whatever it would be 15 years from now; whatever was in their private pension plan to which they may belong; and whatever they had in savings or in RRSPS. However, the most important part about the way in which most of them would live was what they would receive from OAS, which is now about $269 per month. If the cost of living rises each year for the next 15 years by 3 per cent or more, it will mean that when they retire at age 65, 15 years from now, the value of their old age pension through OAS will in fact be just about half what it is now. This has tremendously disturbing implications for all those people who are trying to plan for their retirement, people who were hoping, expecting and were led to believe that they would live on retirement in some comfort and dignity. This deindexation of OAS destroys that belief.
If it is right or necessary to deindex OAS, I ask government Members whether there is anything wrong with deindexing the Canada Pension Plan. Will we get that next year? At the same time the Government is doing this to ordinary people, it is giving rich people the opportunity to invest $15,500 in RRSP plans each year. Who can invest $15,500 in an RRSP each year-only people with very high incomes.
The former Liberal Government lowered the marginal rate at which high income people paid income tax. Now they are being told not to worry about paying that lower rate of income tax, and that they can avoid paying any income tax, while in high income brackets and before retirement, on $15,500. This will give them a tax break of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $6,000 or $7,000 per year. Let us compare that with what the Government is saying to old age pensioners.
It has been estimated that this reduction or deindexation of old age pensions will save the Government $1.6 billion, but of course that will be taken away from old age pensioners. At the same time-and I do not have the time to discuss it today, but I will certainly do so on another occasion-the Government has given tax concessions and tax breaks to the wealthy. The Government will lose $1.4 billion in revenue and the wealthy will gain almost that amount. In other words, the Government is saying that it will take away $1.6 billion from old age pensioners and give almost that amount to the very wealthy. That is where the Government wants to take the people of Canada. The Government cannot fool old age pensioners. It cannot hide the facts from them. Our pensioners may be old, but they are not stupid.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right. I must have hit a nerve because suddenly Conservative Members are interjecting. It will take a few months for old age pensioners to realize what is happening. They will know what has happened when they go to the supermarket to do their shopping and find that the price of groceries-meat, milk, cheese, everything-has risen, and when they receive their pension cheques and discover that they are not receiving the kinds of increases they used to get until now. They will not have to depend on the Members of the Opposition. They will not have to depend on old age pension organizations, which are already speaking on their behalf. Each and every one of them will know what has happened because they can clearly see what has happened.
A large percentage of our old age pensioners, particularly single women, widows, those who have never been married, and those who stayed home while they were married bringing up their children and who have certainly not worked in recent years, are living in poverty now, It is a sad fact that we really do not know how they live. We do not know how bad it is for them.
I see that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) is here in the Chamber, Mr. Speaker. Since Parliament will not be sitting in July, I invite the Hon. Member to spend a half a day with me to visit some of the soup kitchens operating in our great City of Winnipeg. Let us go to the soup kitchen off Broadway which is operating in the Broadway Optimist Building. Let us visit the Salvation Army and some of the native centres which are feeding people. Let us visit those Catholic churches which are handing out parcels of food, groceries and canned goods. Let us talk to the people at these centres. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine and I could urge the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) to do the same type of thing in Toronto. It will be seen that there are hundreds of thousands of people in this wealthy country who are living in conditions akin to the way people live in the Third World.
In Winnipeg, we have a successful school nutrition program in place. When it was first started, many people said it was not necessary. It was said that this was not the responsibility of the schools. There are young people in Winnipeg whose one and only nutritious meal a day comes from the school. I say that is a disgrace. It is a disgrace to every Canadian. It is a disgrace to every Member of Parliament that this type of situation can exist in our country.
I say to the Members of the Conservative Party: Go out and look at what is happening. Go out and see how people are living. If those Members have any kind of heart, they will say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), "You are moving in the wrong direction." We cannot, in all conscience, permit so many people to continue in the way they are living, not if we have any shred of compassion, any shred of decency.
I would like to deal with what the Budget means for
children. What we have in place is a clearly regressive plan. By
the very calculations of the Minister of Finance, there will be a withdrawal of some $15 million from families in the period 1985-86 and some $40 million in the period 1986-87 because of cut-backs in the family allowance program. These family allowances are being cut back because we are abandoning their indexation. In fact, the purchasing power of that money has lost one-third of what it could buy 10 years ago. The child tax exemption is being significantly reduced through this Budget. The child tax credit has been significantly altered through a reduced income threshold for qualifiers and through reduced indexing.
I would now like to deal with poverty in families. According to the report to which I referred earlier, the poverty rate for a family with one child increased by 17.2 per cent from 1980 to 1983. The poverty rate for a family with two children increased by 25.7 per cent from 1980 to 1983. The poverty rate for a family with three or more children increased by 33 per cent from 1980 to 1983. These are shocking figures. I urge the Government to consider the real situation and increase the disposable income of people in low income brackets instead of decreasing it, as has been done through the proposals in the Budget.
I suggest we should not be thinking about increasing regressive sales taxes on essentials. We should be removing these taxes. We should be removing the sales tax from the important and necessary items required by all families. We should not be increasing these taxes. In conclusion, I say again that this Budget is probably the worst I have ever had to deal with in my more than 20 years in Parliament.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Hon. Member's speech, I found it regrettable that all he had to offer was doom and gloom. It is unfortunate that he dwelt on the negatives and the past. We have a Budget which sets a new direction, one which creates a spirit of optimism and hope. I would ask the Hon. Member to consider that.
I sincerely believe the reason the New Democratic Party is suffering at the polls is because of the negative approach taken in looking at the situation from a textbook perspective as opposed to the real world perspective. 1 would ask the Hon. Member to consider looking in the new direction we are setting for Canada. I ask him to do this objectively. I ask him to join with us in giving all Canadians a new future and new hope.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson) says that the Budget and his Government are taking Canada in a new direction. There is not very much new about the Budget. Several years ago, when Mrs. Thatcher was first elected, she started to carry out the very same measures which this Government is proposing. I suggest the Hon. Member look to what has happened in Great Britain where unemployment is at an all time high.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All time high! It is the worst it has ever been.
June 3, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, 1 think you are right. It is the worst it has ever been. It is certainly worse than the situation which existed during the time of the Great Depression in the 1930s. 1 would ask the Hon. Member to look at the situation in Germany. A few years ago, German voters defeated a social democratic Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Turfed them out!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An Hon. Member says, "Turfed them out!" That is a true statement. They had every right to do that in a democratic system. It was assumed, and reported by all the so-called experts, that it would be a generation before the social democratic party would come back to form the Government in Germany. The present German Government is following the same type of policies which this Government is proposing for Canada. Recently, elections were held in the two largest states in Germany. Some two years after the election, the popularity of the government party has dropped by some 7 per cent.
I wish to make one more prediction for the Hon. Member. If it were not illegal, I would like to make a bet with him. I am prepared to make a small wager with the Hon. Member that in a year from now, because of this Government's policies, there will be 100,000 more people unemployed than there are at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Here we come with pearls of wisdom.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His sincerity is unquestionable, unlike that of the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn). I would like to say one thing about the approach taken by the Hon. Member. Certainly we have problems in this country. There is no question about that. However, the deficit is growing at an unconscionable rate. We are now paying 25 per cent in interest payments alone on the deficit. This leaves us with 75 per cent to spend on the various programs of the federal Government.
All I hear from members of the New Democratic Party is that we should be spending more and that we should not be paying any attention to the deficit, except in one area. They say that we should cut out defence, get out of NATO and get out of NORAD. That is the only area in which they suggest we cut expenditures.
If we go on running up our debts at this crazy breakneck speed, the senior citizens and the health care and post-secondary education programs and the other myriad of programs that come from the federal Government will suffer. They will suffer even more if we do not tackle the problem now so that down the road we can assure the senior citizens and all those people who need our help that it will be there for them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course we have a large deficit
about which we should all be concerned. I would ask the Hon.
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
Member to think about why we have this very large deficit. I say to him that we have this large deficit not because the Government is spending too much money and not because the Government is providing too many services, but because there are a million and a half people who are unemployed.
I urge the Hon. Member to read an article which appeared in the New York Times a few days ago, a copy of which 1 can send to him. The article was about a report from the OECD. What the OECD predicted for Canada next year was that this country would have a rate of unemployment of 11.5 per cent or 11.6 per cent and that that would be the highest rate of unemployment of any country in the OECD. That is not my estimate, that is the estimate of the OECD.
Let me deal for a moment with the deficit. We have a deficit because we have an unemployment rate which is over 11 per cent. There are a million and a half people who are unemployed. Those people are either drawing unemployment insurance benefits or welfare payments. We have a deficit in the unemployment insurance account of $5 billion or $6 billion, I have not looked at the exact figures lately. If one million out of the 1.5 million unemployed were working rather than unemployed, they would not be drawing unemployment insurance payments and they would not be drawing welfare payments. They would be working and they would be paying income tax. They would have the money to purchase things and those purchases would generate sales taxes, both federal and provincial. If one million of the 1.5 million people who are now unemployed were working, the deficit would be quite small.
It is much more important to deal with unemployment than it is to make the number one issue the reduction of the deficit. That is what the Conservative Party and the Prime Minister promised during the election campaign, when he promised "Jobs, Jobs, Jobs". Since the election campaign, unemployment has been forgotten by the Government and they tell us we must now concentrate on reducing the deficit. We are going to do that on the backs of the poor and the old.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) agrees that the problem is the lack of jobs. However, we differ about the methods that should be used to solve the problem. In 1979, when the Conservative Party was in Government for a few short months, the deficit was $11 billion. Today it is $35 billion. A lot of money has been spent in the interim, but the employment situation has not improved. Obviously we must change our methods.
We are trying to create jobs because we believe that in the chicken and egg situation, the chicken is private enterprise and it, rather than the state, must lay the golden egg that will create the jobs. The Hon. Member believes that it is the state that should create the jobs. However, when the state does that, the jobs do not last.
I have heard some of the Hon. Member's colleagues ask how we can talk about reducing the deficit and giving incentives to industries when we have full capacity or close to full capacity in some of our industries. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Toupirt
North does not seem to realize that we have structural problems. We have capacities in industries which do not have markets. We must find new industries for which we have markets so that we can sell our goods and create the jobs we need. We agree on the problem. We simply differ on the method that should be used to solve it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course we agree on the problem and of course we disagree on the method. The method of this Government has been tried in Great Britain and in Germany. It would have been tried in the United States in a more obvious way than it has been tried there. The United States has avoided the kind of problem with which we will soon be faced because that country, under the leadership of President Reagan, has pumped billions of dollars into defence. This has been called by some who are better economists than l "military Keynesianism".
This Government is proposing to follow the words of President Reagan who has said that they must deal with the deficit. But under President Reagan, the United States has the biggest deficits it has ever had. If we follow that prescription, then a year from now, as I mentioned to the Hon. Member's colleague, there will be much more unemployment.
