subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget speech and the Budget papers demonstrate, in my opinion, an attitude on the part of the Progressive Conservative Government and its Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that is realistic, courageous and honest. This Budget reflects a new vision of Canada.
The Budget reflects a realistic attitude because it truly addresses the deficit. The present Government knows that if it does not reduce future deficits and the upward spiral of the national debt, it will inevitably be necessary to increase taxes drastically and make cuts in basic social programs. The present Government is very reluctant to take such measures, because a drastic increase in taxes would have a disastrous effect on the country's productivity and our international competitive position, and as for cutting social services, the human cost would be totally unacceptable. The Budget is realistic because it takes a balanced and sensible approach. It is balanced because tax increases will be phased in gradually up to 1990-91.
The Budget is sensible because as we all know, increasing taxes too quickly would have undesirable effects on our economic growth. It is sensible, Mr. Speaker, because it leads the way to further reduction of our deficit. It is sensible, Mr. Speaker, because it takes into consideration the position of Canada's economy vis-a-vis that of the United States. On a per
capita basis, our national debt is twice that of the United States. However, our tax field here in Canada does not afford the same possibilities for taxation as in the United States, because much of the territory is already covered.
Mr. Speaker, this Budget is courageous because it increases indirect and direct taxes, a measure that is not particularly popular with the general public. We must act immediately, however, because the Budget reduces Government spending and in so doing, has a direct impact on groups with specific interests and privileges.
We are also well aware, Mr. Speaker, that such "house cleaning" measures may alienate certain interest groups. The present Government, however, will continue to act in the best interests of all Canadians.
This Budget reflects an honest attitude on the part of the Government, Mr. Speaker, because it candidly discusses the not very encouraging state of our finances. Today, we have an annual deficit of $35 billion. We have a national debt of over $190 billion. Twenty-five per cent of all Government spending now goes to service debt charges. In five years, if no action is taken immediately, this will rise to nearly 46 per cent.
I also want to say that this Budget reflects a new vision of Canada, a faithful reflection of the Throne Speech and the financial statement, tabled last November. Mr. Speaker, this Budget gives form to the new vision of Canada that all Canadians supported by electing a Progressive Conservative Government. A new vision of Canada, where politicians and public servants will have a more modest role to play. No more almighty government, no more omnipresent government! A new vision of Canada where individuals and the private sector will play an increasingly important role. The birth of a State that creates freedom and the spirit of entrepreneurship. A new vision of a Canada where the State will act as a mediator, and the ultimate goal will be our common prosperity.
The Speech from the Throne, last November's financial statement and the present Budget have proposed a new direction for Canada: a balanced vision of a strong and united Canada where the provinces are given their due.
I would like to discuss some of the principles contained in this Budget. I also intend to provide evidence to support these principles.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, this Budget constitutes a turning point in Canada's social and economic evolution. It uses the living strength of the market and banks on the entrepreneurship of Canadian men and women by placing at their disposal new financing tools and sources.
Let us look at these new financing tools and sources. There is the $500,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption for an individual taxpayer. This proposal promotes risk-taking and investment in small and medium-size businesses in order to create permanent jobs.
June 3, 1985

In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I would like to set the record straight on two points, one of which concerns an allegation made by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Gar-neau). He said in this House last week that such a proposal would give rise to land speculation. This allegation surprises me all the more as the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides was once Minister of Finance in Quebec. Mr. Speaker, under the Income Tax Act and Canadian law, and this is very clearly explained in the interpretation bulletins of the Department of Revenue, any gain derived from any land, speculation, any gain derived from the sale of real estate involving speculation, is not taxed as a capital gain, but as income, fully taxable income. This means, Mr. Speaker, that this $500,000 capital gains tax exemption does not apply to such gains. It is quite untrue to suggest the contrary. I also heard certain Members and other people say that this proposal might promote speculation or the purchase of real estate in the United States or in other countries. Once again, Mr. Speaker, under Canadian tax laws and international tax treaties, which avoid double taxation in principle, if someone invests in the United States or elsewhere, the resulting capital gains will be taxed in that country. Here, in Canada, we are taxed on our total income, domestic and otherwise. What we do is to take these gains, to tax them in Canada and to apply the foreign tax credit against the taxes payable in Canada. Mr. Speaker, this proposal to abolish the capital gains tax not only will fail to promote investments in real estate in other countries, but will have the opposite effect and allow investments to remain in Canada, for the simple reason that there will be no capital gains tax payable in this country, while a capital gains tax will be payable in other countries but no tax credit applicable in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the cost of this measure will be $550 million in 1985 and $700 million in 1986. The principle is as follows: instead of collecting this potential revenue, we are relying on the private sector to put it to good use. We feel the economic impact will be greater this way than if the Government had spent the same amount of money. Mr. Speaker, this has been amply demonstrated by the results of the previous Liberal Government's way of doing things.
I realize I do not have much time left, but we have a number of measures I could mention to support the first principle 1 mentioned earlier. There is the new tax credit encouraging individuals to invest in labour-sponsored venture capital funds, a measure that will help create new jobs and help maintain existing ones, a measure, Mr. Speaker, that demonstrates the cordial relationship between the new Federal Government and the provinces.
There is also an extremely innovative measure aimed at tapping a new source of financing, in a fact, a very important new source of financing, for small and medium-sized businesses that are Canadian-controlled and located here in Canada. This measure makes available, as a source of financ-
The Budget-Mr. Toupin
ing, funds in registered retirement savings plans, registered retirement income funds, deferred profiteering plans and pension plans. A very innovative measure, Mr. Speaker, that will help create permanent jobs.
There is also the measure concerning housing loans aimed at facilitating mobility, which will help both the employee and the companies involved.
I could go on to mention the new tax measures for the oil industry in connection with the National Energy Program. A while ago, I heard the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) claiming that the Progressive Conservative Government was subsidizing the oil industry. I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the subsidies that were paid to the oil multinationals were in fact paid by the previous Liberal Government. We are eliminating those subsidies. As a result, in 1985-86 we will be saving $800 million. In 1986-87 we will be saving another $800 million. I felt I had to set the record straight, Mr. Speaker, despite the fact the Hon. Member is not in the House at this time.
Once again, I would like to mention that the National Energy Program was designed to subsidize the price of oil.
Mr. Speaker, new taxes were levied and new grants awarded under the National Energy Program. Oil prices were subsidized to prevent them from going up. At the same time, a litre of gas was selling for half the price in the United States, and without any grants either.
Since I have only about five minutes left, I will deal more quickly with my second point. This Budget faithfully reflects Canada's changing approach to social services. Those measures include assistance to poorer families through the child tax credit of $70 in 1986 and $35 in 1987 and subsequent years. Help will be extended to the voluntary sector, among other things by making it easier to donate to charitable organizations. More handicapped will receive assistance since the basic definition is now less restrictive so that 185,000 rather than
65,000	people will be entitled to claim the $2,590 exemption for 1986. Through tax incentives, Canadian men and women will be encouraged to save more for their retirement years, and well-to-do individuals, major corporations and financial institutions will pay more taxes.
My third point, Mr. Speaker, is that the Budget shows our growing concern for the situation of women and provides a retirement income plan which is more equitable for women. Here are some of the highlights: the survivor's pension will continue to be paid in case of remarriage; pension plans will have to pay benefits to the wife of a deceased pensioner; the value of pension rights and existing pensions will be split between spouses upon divorce, separation or a break in common law relationships, subject to a court decision; an additional $900 million earmarked for job creation by the
5346

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Toupin
Department of Employment and Immigration in 1985, and again the same amount in 1986-87, Mr. Speaker.
The fourth point is that the Budget makes for greater tax equality by asking rich people to pay their fair share. The tax credit for scientific reearch-a tax loophole as big as they come, Mr. Speaker-has been eliminated. Some $100 million will be recouped in 1986 by doing away with tax shelters where a tax credit was given to the investor or the individual who bought certain things. This relates, for example, to companies offering leisure services, pleasure boats, recreational vehicles, hotel accommodation and the like.
Amendments which will prevent taxpayers from avoiding tax by splitting income between spouses.
A minimum income tax.
Next to last point, Mr. Speaker. This budget proposes measures to streamline the tax system, rationalize the many government programs, encourage financial responsibility and reduce the enormous size of the bureaucracy.
I wish I could mention measures to support this statement, but I am running out of time.
Sixth point, Mr. Speaker. This budget takes into account the inequalities between the regions, especially the more disadvantaged ones.
Again, I could provide concrete proof of this.
As a seventh and final point, Mr. Speaker. In this budget, we practice what we preach by asking senators and former members of Parliament for additional sacrifices, in the direction shown by the Speech from the Throne and last November's economic statement. In this regard, I should like to remind the House that the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has asked Canadian men and women for sacrifices. He was the first to lead the way by initiating a 15 per cent put in his own ministerial salary.
Finally, by way of conclusion, the Progressive Conservative government has asked all Canadians, especially those with higher incomes, to make sacrifices themselves, in order to put Canada back on the right track financially and to ensure for our country a sound economic future.
Following a dramatic turn all the while striking a happy medium, the Progressive Conservative government is striving for economic renewal as a source of real and permanent jobs and increased and enhanced basic social programs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for recognizing me in the waning hours of the Budget debate. I recognize that in this, the last lap, spirits are flagging a little and, from what I heard in the last speech, some of the acumen is obviously growing weaker as time progresses.
It is a privilege for me, as it is for every Member of Parliament, to speak in a debate which is certainly one of the high festivals of parliamentary democracy. It is a very important event in the parliamentary calendar. Not only are we debating specific measures of economic initiative, we also have the opportunity to ferret through the various contradictions and high-falutin but broken promises made over the years in order to get to the gist of what the Tories are trying to achieve in their Budget.
A Budget is probably more than the sum of its parts. It is
not just a series of strung-out measures. If you bring them all
June 3, 1985

together, it reveals an approach or the blue-print of what a particular Government is trying to achieve for the country. Therefore, we must read into the Budget what it tells us about the modern day conservatism, the new "Mulroney revolution", the new social aura that has been heralded far and wide as being the hallmark of the new Government.
Unfortunately, there has been one basic mistake. We have been trying to analyse the Budget by finding some unifying or organizing principle in economic textbooks. We have tried to decide whether it is a form of Reaganomics, Keynesian, supply side, or a Thatcherism. This Budget does not fit any of those current definitions. It is impossible to go into economic textbooks and find a proper definition of this Budget. One must really go into the works of fiction. One must look at how our novelists see things in order to properly describe what the Government is trying to achieve.
This weekend I had the opportunity to reread some novels which I thought might give me a better sense of perspective. As 1 first reached into my bookshelf, I saw a novel which cut through all the confusion, obfuscation, and public relations to get to the heart of the matter. It was a wonderful novel written in the 1920s by Sinclair Lewis called Babbitt. All of a sudden it struck me that the Budget is all about Babbittry. This Budget was not conceived in terms of the broad range and perspective of all Canadians. It was conceived by the Babbitt minds of our country in the private schools, private clubs and private boardrooms. It was not done in a malicious or malevolent way, but in a narrow-minded way that does not see the full range of concerns anxieties, hopes, and fears of Canadians. It was conceived in the hothouse atmosphere of a very restricted business community which wants to be the economic elite to lead the salvation.
It was no accident that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in one of his all too frequent mistaken statements, once again told us the truth. He did not think we had enough rich people in Canada to supply the tax revenue. That clearly described the whole problem. The Government really believes, as Babbitt did in the 1920s, in a form of social Darwinism. It believes in some kind of natural order of economic elite that will make decisions for the rest of Canadians.
When the Government talks about inspiring and stimulating Canadians to produce better, it is talking about a very narrow range of Canadians. It is not showing any understanding, comprehension, sensitivity, or feeling for the family of a miner in northern Manitoba who waits week after week for a decision to be made in a Toronto boardroom as to whether the mine will stay open or not, knowing that the Government in Ottawa does not give a damn whether it is open or closed because it is not providing any support or encouragement.
That famous line in the Budget said that the Government will reward success, not subsidize effort. I do not believe there has been a crueller or meaner statement issued by a Minister of Finance in the history of this Parliament. That goes right back to the philosophy of the 1920s that there is an economic jungle
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
out there and only the fittest will survive. The Government is going to reward the survivors, but the rest of them can take their lumps as they may.
This Government does not care much about those people who have to strive in other ways. It does not care much about a young family that wants to buy a home. With one stroke of the pen in the Budget, the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan was wiped out. That was the one avenue through which young families could hope to put money aside as an incentive to eventually get their own homes.
There is probably no more deep-rooted feeling of concern and interest of young Canadians than to acquire a stake in their own community. What does that matter to the Minister of Finance or the Government? Those young people do not play squash at the Albany Club, so why bother with them? Well, they represent a large majority of young Canadians who are trying to achieve something with important economic benefits. That young family who would have some day bought that home would have provided the market for the lumber, craftsmen, and tradesmen which would generate the economy.
What does the Government care about the young farmer in western Canada or southwestern Ontario who has been striving to keep his head above water against drought, falling commodity prices, and hard to achieve capital? Those farmers looked hopefully toward the recommendations of the Commons committee and listened to the promises made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the election campaign. He said he was out to help the farmers, and in this Budget they got higher fuel taxes and higher user fees. The only assistance they will get is if they sell their farms to a big corporate business. There is no assistance for the farmer who wants to stay in business to keep growing his commodities and developing his property. That is not the interest or concern of this Government.
The single parent mothers in downtown Winnipeg have always felt that the federal Government had a basic willingness and generosity to assist them in raising their children. The Minister of Finance tells us how he has increased the child tax credit. However, he does not explain that the figures of his own budget paper indicate that by 1990 some $550 million will disappear from the family trust in the federal Budget. It will no longer be there to help children or to keep families together. It will just disappear. If you combine the deindexation of the family allowance and the child tax credit and the reduction of the exemption, the net loss to lower income families in the country is substantially more than if things had remained the way they were. Do not believe the Minister of Finance when he tries to throw up a dishonest smoke, screen which is fooling a lot of Canadians. It is once again the young Canadian families who will suffer from the measures of this Budget.
What about the young people who are looking forward to achieving new skills and abilities to meet the world of change in which they live? What more important investment can any Government make than an investment in people? The last speaker proudly beat his chest and said that the Government is going to spend $900 million next year on training. However, in

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
the previous Liberal Government, $1.4 billion was spent on job training and creation. How can the Government justify a net reduction in this year of $75 million? That affects the women who are trying to get back in the workforce. They are not being accepted in our community colleges because there is no allowance for them, and still the Government cuts $75 million from that budget. The Government cut the direct assistance to provincial Governments to build new classrooms and provide new laboratories and technical equipment to allow workers to be retrained for the new world in which we want to live.
The Government does not want a new world. It wants to return to the age of Babbittry, back to the 1920s. It does not want to help people to deal with the new world of change. It only wants to ensure that its friends in the investment clubs are happy and that the security funds are satisfied. The Government says it is making these changes to raise the money to reduce the deficit.
However, it will not reduce the deficit. The money which is being denied to senior citizens, young families and housing will be used to pay the $2 billion price tag for the Western Accord and the capital gains investment of $700 million. It has nothing to do with deficit reduction. I suggest that Tory backbenchers conduct their own study because they will see that the budget papers say that the deficit reduction of two billion dollars will come from "better management practices". Those practices involve a classic example of paper shuffling. The Government will not have Supplementary Estimates and will not provide any inflationary increases. The Government will not realize a saving of $2 billion from that procedure.
The Government is not really interested in economic growth. Growth is not simply generated by giving a tax relief to the investment community. Businesses grow when there is a market and people can buy goods and services. The removal of $37 billion from consumers between now and 1990 will result in fewer homes, cars, furniture and other products being bought from the small business community. If the business community cannot sell its products, it will not invest new capital, expand factories and develop new products for which there is no market. One must wonder about the strange, neurotic, ideological thinking taking place in the minds of the Cabinet when it reduces consumer demand by $37 million while saying that it wants the economy to grow. One need not be a genius in economics-which the Government obviously is not-to know that there must be a demand factor in the economy.
What sort of factors are there in the Budget? There is the capital gains exemption which has some marginal benefit. However, the Minister has provided a carte blanche capital gains exemption with no rules or conditions. The Minister of Finance does not believe in rules or conditions in his wonderful free enterprise society. Once given these capital gains, will people invest in blue chip stock or in venture capital in a small business? Will they invest in speculation for a quick turnover or for a long term development in small business?
I suggest that the majority of that capital will not go to aid small Canadian businesses, but there will be an increasing inflation in this country because of the speculative fever that will be released by that measure. There will be large investments on the stock market, but the stock market does not create a lot of wealth in the country. Wealth is created by people going to work and by factories expanding. It is not created by a paper economy in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver. While investors have fun creating their mergers and acquisitions, it does not create the wealth. Wealth is created by ensuring that there is a market and that the capital serves that market.
The Budget is not designed for all Canadians but a select and privileged group of Canadians. All budgets should attempt to release those energies of growth that provide a sense of aspiration by Canadians. This Budget does not do so.
The Budget has another great flaw. We hear Conservative members say in the committee and in the House that private enterprise will create the growth in this country. While private enterprise creates growth, it does not do so by itself. The history of this country has been a clear partnership between Government and private enterprise in a mixed economy. The Government has always supplied important investments in transportation, in infrastructure and research and development. It has provided the basic sinews of economic strength that allows the private market to proceed and build.
Private companies do not build the roads, bridges, ports or schools. They cannot supply the type of collective co-operation that only Government can provide. However, the Government is so paranoid about itself that it refuses to recognize that the Government has a constructive and positive role to play in the economy. The Government should be used rather than feared. It can be used to stimulate because it is an investor in the economy.
From the time of the CPR, the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Trans-Canada Highway, the Government has been a major investor. When the Government calculates the deficit figure, it should recognize that part of that deficit goes into long term investments that will create wealth in this country. Government basically supplies what no one else can.
The Government does not recognize the importance of government as an investor in capital goods. The Federation of Mayors and Municipalities released a very important report at their meeting taking place this week in Calgary. The cities of this country will require $12 billion of new capital in order to simply maintain the present sewer and road systems. If those deteriorate, the productivity of this country goes down. The ability of trucks to move goods across rutted roads costs more. Each time there is a pothole, a weak bridge or a sewer that gives out, we are losing in the economy. At a time when we have to be at our competitive best and meet incredible international challenges, we are surrendering one of our advantages, which is a highly modern efficient infrastructure.
When I was the Minister of Transport, we made some major
decisions to invest capital in projects such as the Western rail
system. That is paying off because it will ensure that foreign
June 3, 1985

buyers will have a sure market for our grain commodities. We had the nerve to take that decision. Although it cost money, if we had not made that decision, the ability of the country to maintain a competitive edge in world grain markets would have been sadly reduced.
However, the Government has nothing in its Budget for that kind of capital investment. It has reduced the Budget for the Industrial Regional Development Program by 50 per cent during 1984-85. It has given up on regional development with the assumption that the private market will respond. Will that happen with the private market in Cape Breton? Will it happen with the private market in northern Manitoba? Those are markets which require the full partnership and co-operation between levels of Government and the private sector.
This is not a growth Budget, one that is designed to stimulate growth or even reduce the deficit. Its purpose is to serve the interests of those who already have a certain advantage in this society. Its greatest weakness and its greatest tragedy is that it does not unleash the energies of all Canadians. It does not meet the concerns of workers who must meet new technological change and will need the Government to help them.
The Government has cancelled the Industrial Renewal Board. I must tell those brave Members from Quebec who stand up in support of the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board that it is no longer in the Budget. It has been put out of business. Those Members will have to rewrite their speeches when they go back to their textile towns. There is no mechanism to help those industries modernize.
This Budget does not encompass the aspirations and hopes of all Canadians, but serves the interests of those who already have advantages. Canadians do not want to have their economic future determined by a corporate elite. They have no interest in letting a small, privileged group of Canadians make their decisions. The Budget has provided the subject for the great debate in this country between those who believe that Canada will prosper by making sure everyone is treated equally and fairly and those in the Government who believe that the economic future in this country can be determined just by their friends.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in recognizing your outstanding job on a continuing basis in the chair, 1 am sure you will ignore the clock at 5.45 in acknowledgement of the fact that you have given opposition Parties much more time to speak than they were allotted. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a privilege and honour to serve in this Chamber with you, Sir.
I regret that I cannot say the same about the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). However, there is one area upon which we agree, that is, the belief that a small, select group of people should not govern the nation. This is exactly why his Party was thrown out of office, because a small, select group of people governed the nation. We are taking the reverse approach. We want to consult with Canadians. We want to allow Canadians a greater opportunity to participate in their own affairs.
He asked what we were doing for young people, among other things. Since we became the Government, interest rates have dropped close to three percentage points. That will have a substantial impact on all mortgage holders. In relation to the farming sector-and I will say a great deal more about that sector if I am allowed the time-the Hon. Member indicated that fuel costs have risen, whereas in reality under this Government they have gone down. It is just another area in which opposition Parties are attempting to mislead Canadians with their deceit and dishonesty.
1 do not want to dwell on those matters because I believe that we as a Party are participating in "new time" politics. Canadians want to know for what we stand. We have indicated it on a consistent basis, unlike the opposition Parties which have nothing but criticism for our sound economic proposals. We have come forward with a clear-cut Budget. I am honoured to stand in my place today to endorse the proposals of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) which he started on February 8 and which he brought down in his Budget on May 23.
For the first time we are at a crossroads in the history of our great nation. For the first time we have a sound economic Budget which will restore economic activity in this great country. On September 4, Canadians voted for change. They
The Budget-Mr. Elzinga
voted for a change in the national affairs of our nation. As 1 indicated on November 8, the Minister of Finance began the process of change. On May 23, we saw more of that. Our economic documents are tough but fair.
We recognize that no one wants to pay additional taxes, but 80 per cent of the budgetary deficit reductions are reductions in government expenditures. We are asking all Canadians to participate to a small degree in restoring an economic climate which is suitable and will encourage growth in many sectors- small business, energy and agriculture.
I say in all sincerity-and 1 look at the three opposition Members who are in the House on this important debate- that all of us are in the Chamber because of our deep love for the nation and our deep concern that in some respects we can contribute to making the country a better place for all. Our Budget represented a turning point, whereby in reality Canadians again enjoy the opportunity and freedom to invest money in areas as they see fit.
We are asking the average Canadian family to contribute $1 per day to budgetary deficit reduction and the restoration of our economic activity. I would think that the majority of Canadian families would be happy to contribute, on average, $1 per day so that we can turn around the sad inheritance which we were left by the Liberal Party.
Our Budget tackles three areas-deficit reduction, job creation and more freedom for Canadians to participate in their own investment choices. We have just come through a period of difficulty. Canadians have suffered anxiety, fear and anger at, as my hon. colleague from Calgary just mentioned, the suggestion that this Government attempted to stifle the engine of growth, not only in the energy sector but also in the agricultural sector. In my travels throughout my constituency 1 sense that a mood of optimism and a mood of faith have been restored because of the actions we have taken. We are encouraging that very important engine of growth by reducing the budgetary deficit by some $4.4 billion. The projections indicate that it will be reduced by another $8.3 billion next year, and individual constituents have indicated that that is not enough. We approached it on the basis that we did not want Canadians to suffer any more than was necessary and that we would not hurt them. We have lived up to our commitments.
Our major commitment during the election campaign was budgetary deficit reduction. We indicated that we would create jobs. I recall my friends opposite, on November 8 when the Minister of Finance brought down his economic statement, indicating how many jobs would be lost in Canada. In reality,
100,000	jobs were created because of the incentives we offered to Canadians. We are asking for an act of faith by the business community, to live up to its commitments to the free enterprise system. It is when Government, business, labour and management are working together for the betterment of our country that we will truly succeed.
If budgetary deficits created jobs, as my friends opposite indicate, we would not have any unemployment today. If we look at the record of previous administrations and their budgetary deficit spending, we see that it is unreal. I would feel

June 3, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Elzinga
truly ashamed, if we as the Government did not tackle this area while i was here as a Member of Parliament, to think of the sad legacy we would leave our children.
Our Leader has approached Canadians on the basis of compassion and fairness. We will ensure that those in the lower income levels are cared for. We have made sure that the safety nets remained in place. Individuals opposite have indicated that we cut back on pensions. That is another area in which they are misleading Canadians. The Guaranteed Income Supplement will continue to rise with the full rate of inflation for those individuals who require that safety net. They are spreading all types of falsehoods, simply for their own shallow, political ends.
I recall as a youngster sitting on my father's knee when he indicated why he immigrated to this country. He emigrated from Holland, a country which was liberated by Canadians some 40 years ago, because Canada was a country of hope and of opportunity, a country wherein if one worked, one prospered. However, that opportunity has been stifled by consistent socialist Governments over the last number of years. Canadians are looking to us and expecting us-and we shall deliver- to restore economic stability. I could go through a long list of what is included in the Budget and the number of positive measures which it contains.
I would like to indicate something with respect to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of this nation. Our Prime Minister has a sense of purpose. He is a healer. He has brought together the various regions of our country. He has indicated on a consistent basis that if the candle burns a little brighter in one region, then it burns that much brighter in all our country. He has shown a deep sensitivity to the regions of the country. He has shown a deep sensitivity to the minorities of the country, whether they be religious, linguistic or ethnic. I salute him, as many Canadians do, for his deep, compassionate attitude which he has shown to all parts of our great nation.
I wish to touch upon some of the specific initiatives which are beneficial to the agricultural sector. We have reduced the excise tax on primary fuel. There have been substantial payouts under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) reduced interest rates under the Farm Credit Act. There is a Bill presently before committee which will truly help the red meat industry in Canada. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) has introduced measures with respect to seaway tolls. A substantial item in the Budget deals with the relief of capital gains. My friends opposite cannot say that in every rural community of the country the citizens did not push for the removal of these capital gains.
If one were to review our record of action, one would see investment now in place which will produce jobs for Canadians. We have successful energy agreements in both western and Atlantic Canada. We have made progress in terms of our environment. We have extended the spouse's allowance to some 85,000 individuals in low income brackets. Severance
benefits have been extended. There have been amendments made to the Criminal Code. Over all, in excess of 200,000 jobs have been created.
I wish to close by dealing with two points, Mr. Speaker. The first point is with respect to the appointment process which we have in place and which we as a national Government are exercising. We face criticism from Members of the Opposition with respect to the individuals we appoint. However, to implement the change we have been elected to implement, it is important that we put in place individuals who have the same philosophy as we on this side of the House. There has never been a Prime Minister in the history of this nation who has been so non-partisan in his appointments.
I would like to share with the Members of the House some facts. These are facts with respect to the appointment process. The prime prerequisite to date of every individual who has been appointed is competence. In looking at the list of appointments, there are a number of Liberals and New Democrats of promiment stature who have been appointed to various positions. I am speaking of Senator Pierre De Bane, David Smith and the Hon. Don Johnston, who received Queen's Counsel appointments from our Government. Ms. Sylvia Gold, a well-renowned New Democratic Party supporter, was appointed as chairperson to the Advisory Committee on the Status of Women. The Hon. Bud Drury was appointed to the Official Residences' Commission. Mr. Gerry Kaplan, another prominent NDP supporter, was appointed as co-chairman of the task force on broadcasting. The Hon. Lloyd Francis, another Liberal, was appointed as Ambassador to Portugal. Stephen Lewis, another strong New Democratic Party supporter, was appointed Ambassador to the United Nations.
These are all excellent individuals. We are not so narrowminded as our friends opposite. We seek talent wherever it lies. We have sought talent. The prerequisite with respect to every one of our appointments has been competence. We cannot help if there are more competent Conservatives in the country than there are New Democrats or Liberals.
We can assure you, Mr. Speaker, as we can assure Canadians, that the prime prerequisite for all of these appointments is competence. We will continue, on a competent basis, to appoint individuals to positions of responsibility so that we as a national Party can carry out the mandate which we were elected to carry out on September 4.
